Both GIFs are below.

fighter_flyaway.gif (5.6 s, loops): your fighter starts exactly where it is in the original. It weaves forward, back, up and down over the scrolling scenery, tilting with each move. Then it hits its afterburner, climbs and streaks off the right edge. To make this work I removed the ship from all 20 original frames and rebuilt the clouds behind it, so the background scrolls cleanly once it moves away.

fighter_with_wingman.gif: the same animation, plus a second ship. I can't draw an X-wing because it's a Star Wars design, so I made an original wingman instead: a cream-and-red interceptor with an amber canopy. It flies in from the left, holds formation above your fighter for a bit, then boosts off to the right just before your fighter leaves.

Each file is about 14.7 MB because every frame of the parallax background changes. If that's too big for your site, I can make lighter versions with fewer colors, a smaller size, or WebP/MP4 instead.

You said: make a infinite looping scroll of a beach scene in this same style as the last gif for pokemon to run under with these dimensions

make a infinite looping scroll of a beach scene in this same style as the last gif for pokemon to run under with these dimensions
For a 1920px-wide screen, make it 1920 × 384 (a 5:1 ratio). If it's pixel art, draw it at 480 × 96 and let it scale up 4× with your pixelated class.

How I got there: the top screen in app/page.tsx:122 is full width × 35vh and uses object-cover, so the gif gets cropped to whatever shape the screen is:

┌───────────────────┬─────────────┬────────┐
│ Screen │ Banner size │ Shape │
├───────────────────┼─────────────┼────────┤
│ 1920×1080 desktop │ 1920 × ~378 │ ~5:1 │
├───────────────────┼─────────────┼────────┤
│ 1440×900 laptop │ 1440 × ~315 │ ~4.6:1 │
├───────────────────┼─────────────┼────────┤
│ 390×844 phone │ 390 × ~295 │ ~1.3:1 │
└───────────────────┴─────────────┴────────┘

How your current gifs fit:
- cloud.gif (1152×648, 16:9): on desktop only about the middle 35% of its height shows, so most of it is cut off. It also gets stretched up past its real size.
- night.gif (485×150, ~3.2:1): it's a little too tall for desktop, so the top and bottom get trimmed. It's blown up about 4×, which is fine since it's pixel art.

Tips:
- Keep important things in the middle. On phones only a narrow center strip shows (about 25% of the width), so the sides get cut off.
- Make the gif seamless left to right if you can, since the Pokémon run across it.
- Watch the file size. Next.js doesn't optimize animated gifs, so a 1920-wide gif can get huge. If it goes over about 1–2 MB, use the smaller pixel-art size or switch to an <video autoplay loop muted> with WebP/MP4.
- Small cleanup: the width={100} height={100} props don't do anything there. You could swap them for fill on the <Image>.

Claude responded: I made the beach as pixel art at 480 × 96, ready for your 4× pixelated class.

Ran 9 commands, read a file, shared files
Ran 9 commands, read a file, shared files

I made the beach as pixel art at 480 × 96, ready for your 4× pixelated class. It's a 12-second loop with no visible jump, and the scene wraps seamlessly from left to right.

The scenery moves in layers at different speeds, like the cloud gif. From back to front:

  • Sky and sun: these stay still. A sun glint on the water twinkles below the sun.
  • Clouds: these move slowest.
  • Distant islands and open sea: these move a bit faster, and the sea has rolling wave highlights.
  • Shoreline foam: it slides along and also washes gently in and out.
  • Sand: this is the fastest layer, with palm trees, rocks, shells and starfish. It moves at 4 px per frame (16 px at 4×), so it should feel right for Pokémon running along the bottom third.

The sun, its glint and a rock cluster sit near the center. That middle strip is what shows on phones.

File size: the GIF is 1.6 MB. That's within your limit because only the pixels that change between frames are stored. I also made 1920 × 384 video versions, which are much lighter: about 390 KB for WebM and 515 KB for MP4. The upscaling is already done in those, so they stay crisp without the CSS class:

tsx
<video autoPlay loop muted playsInline className="absolute inset-0 h-full w-full object-cover">
  <source src="/beach_1920x384.webm" type="video/webm" />
  <source src="/beach_1920x384.mp4" type="video/mp4" />
</video>
